articles.title: Fantasy Football Fades: Here are Hayden Winks' least favorite picks by round for 2026
articles.summary: Fantasy football analyst Hayden Winks takes you through players he's fading by round.
articles.body:
My 2026 fantasy football busts are simply based on who I've been drafting the least in my paid leagues. I'll easily clear 200 drafts this season, and the players I've taken in 0-4% of them are the players that you'll see in today's column. If I'm wrong, then I'm literally paying for it.

Round 1: James Cook, BUF (4% exposure) & Justin Jefferson, MIN (7%)

Cook was the RB6 per game last year, even though he led the NFL in rushing yards and carries per game. His 16.0 half-PPR points per game were 2.0 to 5.0 points behind the top-five backs (CMC, Taylor, Bijan, Gibbs and Achane) largely because he hasn't been a pass-catching back to date. That could change, but it makes less sense for that to happen this year with Dalton Kincaid healthier and DJ Moore added. If he is close to the 1.9 receptions per game (RB39), then he doesn't have the ceiling to compete with the potentially elite Gibbs, Nacua, Chase, Bijan, CMC, JT, etc. teams.

Jefferson was the WR31 last year. It will be nowhere near that bad with Kyler Murray, but the fact that this just happened makes him a no brainer for this exercise. I have him 16th overall in half-PPR behind the clear-cut fantasy RB1s. He's a late Round 1 option in full-PPR.

Round 2: Ashton Jeanty, LV (2% exposure) & Josh Allen, BUF

The vague ankle injury is one thing. Jeanty could miss 0-4 games off the bat, and he's at greater re-injury risk upon his return. But Jeanty was on my fade list before the prayer circle. The Raiders will be better than last year, yet still concerning up front, at QB and at WR. They're projected for 19.2 points per game (28th) and all of the RBs near him are in top-16 offenses aside from De'Von Achane. Jeanty is likely good, but I can't say his rookie tape (or advanced metrics ) showed an elite back, where I at least can easily make that case with Achane via tape or numbers. Jeanty's workload will be very large this year, and it could still come down from his rookie year (RB11 usage) with fourth-rounder Mike Washington Jr. providing far more depth than who was behind Jeanty last season when he was the RB16 in half-PPR points per game.

Allen's fade is simply a pricing issue on Yahoo. When he's available at the Round 3/4 turn, I've been taking him about 9% of the time, which is in line with everyone else. But on Yahoo, his ADP is in Round 2. That's just too rich based on the fantasy points over replacement research I've done using half-PPR scoring, where he's finished between 18th and 30th overall in four straight seasons. In full-PPR, his score would be lower. Allen has played at an MVP level with elite red-zone rushing production across those seasons, and he nets out as an early Round 3 pick. It's hard for him to provide as much of an advantage over a suddenly deep fantasy QB pool. I wrote about this concept here .

Round 3: Trey McBride, ARI (2%) & Rashee Rice, KC (1%)

Recent history suggests that we have to be very careful with drafting elite TEs (see chart below). Trey McBride was the exception last year (I had him 13th overall, to be fair), but there are too many new variables to feel confident about a repeat. McBride led the regular season in routes by 63, not just at TE, but all players. The garbage time points were out of control, and the Cardinals were quietly No. 1 in neutral pass rate. That's just not going to happen with coach Mike LaFleur on the sticks and with third overall pick Jeremiyah Love in the backfield. They will be more balanced. They could also be very bad! Arizona is 31st in projected points per game (18.5), only ahead of the Jets, who have just one pass-catcher (Garrett Wilson) drafted in the top-160 picks in fantasy. The Cardinals have three in the top 90. The target competition versus projected touchdowns math is hard to square, even with McBride being one of my absolute favorite players to watch right now.

Rice is still working his way back from a second surgery to his knee. It's easy to forget that happened because we were distracted from him being in jail for 30 days, but two surgeries on the same knee is never great, especially as he's been unable to run without a glitch in camp. ESPN Chiefs reporter Nate Taylor believes it's asking too much for Rice to clear 900 yards this season based on what he's seen in camp. Rice has to be featured in a very distinct role to be as productive as he's been because the rest of his game is quite limited. He's the worst real-life receiver among anyone drafted in the top-60 overall picks in my opinion. The Chiefs seem poised to be more under center and run heavy with Patrick Mahomes returning from an ACL tear and with Kenneth Walker III providing a real rushing threat for the first time since Rice has been around.

This round is great. I don't have any real issues across the board, though Burrow as the QB4 at 48th overall on Yahoo is too rich. He's been the QB5 per game since 2022, but the entire top-20 is within just 3.5 points per game from that. My favorite strategy in redraft is waiting until the Round 8-14 range and grabbing two QBs who are stacked up with the WR/TEs I've drafted. Burrow is somewhat justifiable on Ja'Marr Chase teams in Round 5 in half-PPR, but that's the only time he should be going anywhere near this. I've taken Burrow in 10% of my drafts, but my personal ADP is 65th overall, not in Round 4.

Round 5: David Montgomery, HOU (4%) & Bucky Irving, TB (2%)

Montgomery must overcome his career wear-and-tear along with an OL that's been horrific for the entirety of the C.J. Stroud era. The Texans are 31st in EPA per carry and 22nd in rush yards per game since 2023 when DeMeco Ryans and Stroud were brought to Houston. If Montgomery is Joe Mixon, then I'm wrong. But Montgomery is not paid like Mixon was, nor has had the career Mixon had before his RB9 finish in 2024. The lead back finished outside the top-34 in 2023 and 2025. Woody Marks is a second-year player with a better passing-down profile and improved play between the tackles based on his camp reports and preseason tape. Montgomery's missed tackles per touch rate last year was 18% when it was 27%, 21% and 24% in the previous three seasons, and if he's not clearly better than Marks, then there's no reason to make this a bellcow backfield. Even if he is a workhorse for one more year, the Texans OL is starting an out-of-position rookie center and three potentially washed veterans.

Irving was 65th in rush yards over expected (-29%) and 64th in EPA per carry (-0.21) out of 66 qualifying RBs last season. He wasn't breaking as many tackles and looked worn down. After returning from shoulder and foot injuries in Week 13, Irving lost goal-line carries to the much-bigger Sean Tucker, 6 to 0. Will that stick? Unsure, but the evidence that it's possible is concerning because he's clearly being squeezed by Kenneth Gainwell (two years, $14 million) on passing downs. Even if he escapes both backs in his backfield, Irving will need to stay healthy as a 195-pound rusher with a shoulder history and have the Bucs rebound in general. That 2024 breakout season for Irving happened on an offense that was fourth in scoring (29.0 points per game). Tampa Bay is 18th in projected points (23.3) by the betting markets.

When Rhamondre Stevenson and Henderson were healthy, inside the 5-yard line carries went to the big fella, 12 to 4. When they were both healthy for the four games in the NFL Playoffs, Stevenson outscored him 11.6 half-PPR points per game to 3.4. Yes, that's 3.4 fantasy points per game for Henderson when the Super Bowl run was on the line. Henderson's pass protection failures cost him valuable snaps, and his rushing style proved too boom-bust to give him real volume. Meanwhile, Stevenson was just perfectly fine. In fact, NextGenStats' tracking data had Stevenson with the best rush yards over expected in the NFL. Nothing I've read in camp has suggested that the performance gap has closed. If Stevenson fumbles too often or gets injured, then Henderson is going to absolutely cook. I just can say the same thing about Blake Corum, Kyle Monangai, Tank Bigsby, Mike Washington Jr. and others who go many rounds later.

Round 7: Carnell Tate, TEN (1%) & Jonathon Brooks, CAR

I compared Tate to DeAndre Hopkins, Calvin Ridley and Jeremy Maclin before the draft, as my ninth overall player . He's pretty polished for a 21-year-old early declare but his skill set isn't necessarily fantasy friendly. He mostly plays outside and runs routes on the vertical stem. His speed and tackle breaking is fine, not elite, so there's less incentive to make sure he has two-to-three easy receptions per game like others who have gone as high in the draft. That role for the Titans is going to go to slot Wan'Dale Robinson whether we like it or not. Beyond that, there are real concerns with the Titans. It's the first year in a new scheme, one that we don't even love. The OL might be the worst in the NFL, and Cam Ward stunk behind it last year. Tennessee was 30th in scoring and 30th in passing yards last year. The preseason games haven't eased my concerns with Ward's development. Tate has gone catchless on 25 routes in them.

Brooks has an ADP of 84.7 over the past seven days on Yahoo and it's higher than that on other platforms. His return to play is an awesome story, but multiple ACL tears and almost zero NFL experience is a lot to overcome when the price tag is assuming he's in starting fantasy lineups. I'm not convinced he's the Panthers starter, and the Panthers are not going to be good. They're projected for just 20.8 points per game (26th). Chuba Hubbard is returning to practice shortly and remains on track to play in Week 1. In the last playoff game, Hubbard scored two touchdowns on 17 touches, dusting Rico Dowdle after he returned to pre-injury form. When healthy in 2024, Hubbard was half-PPR's per-game RB12 on RB7 usage, while being the RB4 in rush yards over expected (+24%). Carolina signed him to a four-year, $33 million extension during that stint. The bar to clear Hubbard is higher than we realize. This matters less than anything in this paragraph, but Brooks' preseason tape has been very mediocre. I don't see great athleticism yet, and he's had multiple whiffs in protection.

Round 8: Rico Dowdle, PIT (1%) & George Kittle, SF (2%)

I'm on team Jaylen Warren, as I wrote here .

Kittle is a soon-to-be 33-year-old who had Achilles surgery on Jan. 14. Week 2 will be exactly nine months from that point, and that's the absolute earliest we see skill players come back from it. Most of the time, there is a real ramp-up period in terms of snaps, while efficiency also regresses. That's the part that is concerning for Kittle. Over the past two seasons, Kittle averaged 6.1 targets per game (TE8) and 10.7 yards per target (TE1). If the Achilles tear means he's closer to 5.0 targets per game (TE22) and 8.5 YPT (TE5), then he's averaging only 42.5 yards per game. That feels far more realistic than what a Round 7 price tag suggests.

Round 9: Chris Godwin Jr., TB (1%) & Patrick Mahomes, KC (2%)

Godwin just wasn't anywhere near his usual self in 2025, coming off another devastating injury. It's possible he's just healthier and he rebounds, but that's a dangerous game to play for a 31-year-old with his injury history. Godwin is also playing with a coordinator without the history he's had with the Bucs, and it's hard to review the 2025 tape and not believe that Emeka Egbuka is just another full tier above. I can also make a case for Jalen McMillan. Take Godwin's career-low 1.28 yards per route or Matt Harmon's Reception Perception data as evidence; Godwin's 6th percentile rating against zone and 16th percentile rating against man coverage are nowhere near what Egbuka had (56th and 67th percentile) in a far more difficult outside role within the offense.

Mahomes was the QB10 (on QB15 EPA per dropback) from 2023 to 2024 with this flawed pass-catching group. That was absolutely not his fault, but it happened while largely healthy. Last year's return to fantasy stardom was driven by a career-high 30.1 rushing yards per game, and that's something to entirely fade while coming back from a torn ACL, even if his training camp has gone smoothly. Mahomes will be protected by the call sheet and the Kenneth Walker III signing, to the point that the Chiefs total dropbacks could notably decline. There are too many dual threat QBs or MVP candidate statues who go after Mahomes to make him a priority, especially if fading Rashee Rice.

articles.title: Inspiring story on mental health: “I have the right people around me always and that’s where I stay when people wanna be shitty” - How Brittany Mahomes learned to protect her peace from social media negativity

articles.body: For Brittany Mahomes, being in the public eye has never meant escaping criticism. In April 2022, the entrepreneur opened up about the emotional toll of online negativity during an Instagram Q&A with followers. Her answer offered a candid look at how she dealt with harsh comments, why she stepped back from social media and how the people closest to her became an important source of stability.Brittany Mahomes opened up about mental health and social media pressureThe comments came during an Instagram Q&A in April 2022, when Brittany was still publicly known as Brittany Matthews. A follower asked her how she continued to show “grace in such a hateful world.” Rather than giving a polished response, she acknowledged that handling constant criticism had taken time.Her answer showed that protecting mental well-being did not come easily. She said she had learned to separate what happened online from the life she experienced away from the screen.Brittany wrote:“Honestly, I have no other choice! I would never let people on the internet destroy my peace or effect [sic] my life.”That sentence captured the central idea behind her response. She did not claim that criticism never affected her. Instead, she admitted that learning how to deal with it had been a process.“BUT. It’s been hard, it took time to learn this and still learning at times.”That admission made her message more personal. Social media can make criticism feel constant because there is no clear boundary between public attention and private life. For someone connected to one of the NFL's biggest stars, that pressure can become even harder to escape.Reports from the time confirmed that her remarks were made through Instagram Stories during a fan Q&A.Brittany Mahomes explained why she stepped away from social mediaOne of the strongest parts of Brittany's message was her decision to recognize when she needed distance.She explained that the negativity did not remain at the same level every day. Some periods were worse than others, and she said those were the moments when followers would notice less of her online presence.“It’s always gonna be there, at times its [sic] worse then [sic] others & at those times is when you won’t see me on here or the internet.”She then connected that choice to a broader decision to reduce her time on social media.“Hence why I have taken such huge steps away from social media. It’s a toxic and horrible place at times and those are when I say peace out.”The language was direct, but the idea behind it was simple. She was setting a boundary.Instead of treating constant online engagement as something she had to endure, Brittany chose to step away when it became overwhelming. That approach is particularly relevant in an era when public figures can face a stream of reactions within seconds of posting something.Her comments also showed that taking a break was not necessarily a sign of weakness. For Brittany, it was a way of deciding what deserved her attention and what did not.Contemporary reports from April 2022 preserved the same remarks and placed them in the context of her Instagram Q&A about dealing with criticism.Brittany Mahomes credited her support system for helping her find peaceThe most memorable part of Brittany's response came when she shifted the focus away from social media and toward her life offline.“My world outside of social media is great. I have the right people around me always and that’s where I stay when people on here wanna be sh-tty. Not my problem, bye.”That statement reveals why her support system mattered so much to her.When online attention becomes loud, a strong personal circle can provide something the internet cannot: perspective. Friends and family know the person behind the public image. They are also less likely to judge someone's entire life based on one photograph, comment or moment.Brittany's message was not about convincing every critic to change their opinion. It was about refusing to allow those opinions to control her private life.That distinction matters. Public figures often cannot prevent people from talking about them. What they can control is how much space those voices receive in their own lives.Her decision to focus on the people around her reflected that mindset.Brittany Mahomes turned criticism into a lesson about boundariesBrittany's comments came at a time when she was frequently discussed online because of her relationship with Patrick Mahomes and her own growing public profile. As the wife of an NFL superstar, she had become a familiar figure around the Kansas City Chiefs and on social media.That visibility brought attention, but it also brought scrutiny.Her response offered a glimpse into the less glamorous side of that visibility. Behind the photographs, celebrations and public appearances was someone learning how to manage an environment where opinions could arrive from thousands of strangers.Years later, the comments continue to be referenced because their core message remains familiar: protecting your peace sometimes means knowing when to leave the conversation.Brittany did not suggest that she had mastered the process completely. In fact, she openly said she was “still learning.” That may be the most relatable part of her message.Mental well-being does not always come from finding one perfect solution. Sometimes it comes from making smaller choices repeatedly. Take a break. Spend time with people you trust. Stop reading every comment. Remember that an online opinion does not define your real life.For Brittany, that meant creating distance from the noise and returning to the people and places that made her feel grounded.Her April 2022 Instagram message therefore became more than a response to one follower's question. It was a snapshot of how a young woman navigating intense public attention tried to draw a line between the world watching her and the world she actually lived in.And perhaps that is why her words still resonate. In a culture that often rewards constant visibility, Brittany Mahomes chose something different: stepping away when she needed to, leaning on the people she trusted and refusing to let strangers online determine the quality of her life.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: NFL insider predicts dark-horse team could emerge as AFC champions
articles.summary: One NFL insider thinks that a dark-horse team could win the AFC this year.
articles.body:
We're entering the final week of the NFL preseason, meaning the regular season is just around the corner.

With that in mind, predictions from NFL media members are starting to come out, including which team is the one to beat in the AFC.

NFL Network's Steve Wyche joined Jim Rome on the "Jim Rome Show" on Tuesday and thinks that the Denver Broncos are the team to beat in the AFC this year.

"He's got so much room to grow ( Bo Nix ); he's got so much ability, and now with Davis Webb . who has been his position coach the last couple of years, now designing and calling plays as the OC under Sean Payton, I think it's going to continue to grow. And the fact that he's got Jaylen Waddle at his disposal to go with Courtland Sutton , to go with Evan Engram , and to go with a good offensive line, Denver's the team to beat in the AFC," Wyche said . "We can talk about everybody else; this is the team to beat, and they should've represented the AFC last year had Bo Nix not gotten hurt."

The Broncos got all the way to the AFC Championship Game last year before losing at home to the New England Patriots . Nix broke his right ankle against the Buffalo Bills in the AFC divisional round and wasn't able to play against the Patriots.

He's now fully healthy heading into the 2026 season and will try to take the Broncos even further.

The Broncos will open the 2026 NFL season against the Kansas City Chiefs on Sept. 14. Kickoff will be at 8:15 p.m. ET on ESPN/ABC.

articles.title: Patrick Mahomes voice: Travis Kelce once threw shots at the Kansas City Chiefs QB as the Las Vegas Raiders mocked him with a Kermit the Frog puppet
articles.summary: NFL News: According to Guancheng Wei, Patrick Mahomes’ voice has even been compared to Donald Duck’s. Behind the jokes, however, is a more personal story.In sev.
articles.body: According to Guancheng Wei, Patrick Mahomes’ voice has even been compared to Donald Duck’s. Behind the jokes, however, is a more personal story.In seventh grade, classmates reportedly mocked and imitated Mahomes’ voice, calling him “Duck.” The experience reportedly affected his confidence, and for a long time, he avoided speaking because of the attention his voice attracted.As he grew older, Mahomes slowly accepted that his voice was simply a part of who he was. Still, the imitations followed him into the NFL. Travis Kelce has occasionally mocked Mahomes’ voice for laughs, while teammates have even held contests to see who could produce the best imitation of the Kansas City Chiefs quarterback.What may once have felt like a source of embarrassment has now become something Mahomes handles calmly. And his distinctive voice may even have an advantage on the gridiron, as teammates can reportedly hear his commands clearly amid stadium noise.Why does Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes sound like that?According to USA TODAY NEWS, Patrick Mahomes’ raspy voice has frequently been compared to Kermit the Frog. His voice has been the subject of jokes for years, and even his former High School coach, Reno Moore, remembered Mahomes trying to disguise it as a teenager by deepening his voice to change how he sounded.Experts say changes in how a person speaks are possible. Dr. Randal Paniello, a renowned voice and airway specialist, explained that changing tongue position could alter Mahomes’ tone. Both non-surgical and surgical methods can modify vocal pitch, although a permanent change may require considerable practice.Brendan Houdek, a licensed speech-language pathologist and voice coach, has worked with clients with voices similar to Mahomes’ and said some people can see results after just a few sessions.Dr. Steven Zeitels suggested that Mahomes’ vocal quality could be influenced by the shape of his nose and mouth rather than his vocal cords. The strain from years of calling plays could also contribute to his deep, sometimes rumbling voice. Although Zeitels has not examined Mahomes personally, he believes the quarterback’s distinctive tone is largely a product of his anatomy.Travis Kelce and the Raiders have all joined the voice jokesMahomes has also shown that he can take the jokes in stride.Travis Kelce has occasionally poked fun at his quarterback’s distinctive voice, while former Chiefs teammate Tyreek Hill has also been part of the light-hearted teasing over the years. But perhaps one of the most memorable jokes came from the Las Vegas Raiders.The Raiders once trolled Mahomes with a Kermit the Frog puppet dressed in a Kansas City Chiefs jersey. Mahomes did not appear to let the joke bother him. Instead, he responded the way he knows best: on the football field.Mahomes and the Chiefs defeated the Raiders twice during the regular season, giving the quarterback a fitting response to the trolling. After an AFC Championship victory, Mahomes even posted an image of Kermit the Frog sipping tea with the caption, “I’ll see y’all in New Orleans.”According to USA TODAY, Mahomes may never completely escape the Kermit comparisons. However, former Kermit voice actor Steve Whitmire once offered a humorous consolation: at least Mahomes does not sound like Miss Piggy.Patrick Mahomes has learned to embrace his voiceKansas City Star’s Vahe Gregorian wrote in October 2018 that Patrick Mahomes had been teased about his voice in seventh grade. That is often an age when voices begin to change, or when children become especially quick to notice anything that makes someone sound different.Mahomes, however, eventually learned to embrace what once made him insecure.In a 2018 interview with ESPN, Mahomes said, “It’s just something that I’ve kind of embraced.” He later explained that the key was simply being comfortable with himself.“Just being comfortable with yourself. I mean, it’s me. It’s who I am. So, I’m never going to be insecure about it. I just kind of embrace it and keep going.”For Mahomes, the voice that once made him a target of jokes has become an unmistakable part of his identity. Whether people hear Donald Duck, Kermit the Frog, or simply Patrick Mahomes, the Kansas City Chiefs quarterback has made one thing clear: he is no longer interested in changing who he is.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Fantasy Football: Should you try Zero RB this season? Here's everything to know for 2026
articles.summary: Fantasy football analyst Chris Allen breaks down Zero RB for 2026.
articles.body:
My mom taught my siblings and I almost every card game when we were younger. She didn't grow up with much, but you could find a pack of bikes on any counter at my grandma's house. Our favorite game was Rummy. Building runs or finding sets and racking up points until my diabolical mother dropped the concept of "gin" on us.

The first time she dropped all her cards and declared herself out, my jaw dropped. I was mad and impressed simultaneously. Since then, I've added the (relatively) extreme strategy to my play. When it works, my wife threatens me with the couch. In other cases, I'm in a different kind of trouble.

That's the Zero RB draft approach in a nutshell.

It looks drastic. But if it works, your leaguemates praise you for your boldness. In either case, let's dig into the basics and how we can apply it in 2026.

So, What's This Zero RB Thing All About?

To be honest, the name of the tactic should nudge you in the right direction. But I'll use a recent example to highlight the core premise:

Unfortunately, an injury like Ashton Jeanty's happens every preseason. One of our high-priced skill players suffers an injury or finds themselves in a situation where the potential for them to miss a significant period of the season exists. The reaction from fantasy managers is, well, predictable.

"This is why you don't draft until the end of the preseason."

"Always get your RB's backup just in case!"

The "RBs Don't Matter" crowd comes alive in these situations. Drafters who were diligently snagging Mike Washington Jr are geniuses. Accordingly, we learn (the hard way) about one of the main tenets of Zero RB.

The number of RBs with bellcow opportunity shares declines faster than their receiver counterparts. This trend seeds the notion to wait. Of course, the Jeanty to Washington scenario is an abnormal occurrence. Let's find something more reasonable.

There was a two-round gap in ADP between the New England RBs at the start of the offseason. But as more information came out, the delta decreased. More importantly, managers who opted for a WR over TreVeyon Henderson gain two edges. One, they now have the benefit of a player with a greater chance at more weekly touches. And two, Stevenson's access to high-leverage touches at a cheaper draft cost gives them a value surplus.

Zero RB aims at avoiding the "risks" of early-round rushers who could turn into busts by focusing on the position with more players getting a high-end workload: wide receivers. As the chart above indicates, our greatest shot at finding pass-catchers earning WR1 treatment stays open well past where the RB pool has dried up. So, until then, holding off on grabbing your RB1 should ensure your roster has the receiving firepower to take on the rest of your league.

Like learning gin rummy for the first time, you'd be hard-pressed not to try and replicate the method on your own. However, like all things, there are some caveats.

So, you've got the idea surrounding Zero RB. Vector your roster's strength to be at WR, take swings at rushers who could turn into weekly contributors later, and profit. But sometimes our attempts look like that scene in The Waterboy where another college puts their towel boy on the field . There's some nuance to this worth reviewing before heading into your draft.

Can I draft a "onesie" position? Or should I stick to WRs?

Like any confident analyst, I'll give you the best answer I can. It depends.

I built a points-above-replacement model to measure value as a function of draft cost. Essentially, it checks to see if you're getting something now that you can't get later. Anyway, two takeaways here.

First, yes, nabbing a QB or TE within the first six rounds has its merits. But the timing matters. Taking the first or second quarterback off the board is different than the QB4 or QB5. And TEs actually tick up in value (over WRs!) in Rounds 4 and 5. But look at the orange line for the larger point.

RBs still have value in the early rounds. In fact, since 2021, at least one eventual top-three PPR RB finisher was drafted inside the first round. Admittedly, this doesn't solve our "elite RB scarcity" problem. But it does leave the door open for considering a single ball carrier to open our draft (i.e., the Hero RB build).

Oh, I understand. RBs lose their jobs more often, so take a receiver instead.

Anecdotally, that's what news like Jeanty's injury causes us to believe. Or take Bucky Irving splitting with Rachaad White and Sean Tucker down the stretch of '25. Nobody wanted to believe a change was happening until we saw it each week. However, those cases are in the minority.

I went through the weekly usage reports and tracked how often an RB1 or WR1 maintained their role. A one-game blip didn't count. Tee Higgins sometimes outshines Ja'Marr Chase. But a multi-game adjustment of their positions on the totem pole would cause a ruckus. Regardless, RBs who got the nod to be the top option kept it more often than receivers. All of which lends more credence to the suggestion that there's more stability to RBs than we give them credit.

But WR output is more stable in the early rounds, right?

That's the natural extension of the workload decline that we laid out earlier. Increased touches lead to greater scoring. As a result, if more WRs with a higher share of touches are available early, they should be putting up more points than their ball-carrying brethren. The data says otherwise.

Using the same weekly dataset, I calculated how much each player bounces around every Thursday, Sunday and Monday. First, the averages between the two positions are essentially the same. But even their week-to-week swings line up. So, taking an RB or two to kick off your draft can still work.

Now, with an honest evaluation of Zero RB, let's apply it.

To recap, Zero RB doesn't have a stringent requirement on when to take your first rusher. It's more about understanding where the projectable opportunities dissipate. But if history gives us any clues, that happens toward the end of the early rounds.

I pulled the same value from our "bellcow workload bar" earlier and isolated the running back values. The hit rate drops by half between Rounds 4 and 7. Said another way, we're almost out of viable options. But we can't just draft a guy because he has "RB" next to his name.

I went back to my study of the RB Dead Zone to pull out a profile of a rusher with the potential to outkick their ADP. And the summary didn't stop at their intrinsic abilities. Their environment matters, too. However, since we'll be pulling from the RB well deep into drafts, I looked at ball carriers with late-round draft prices, too. Coincidentally, the same metrics floated to the top.

Intuitively, this makes sense. After the elites go in the first few rounds, we're buying as many narratives as possible for how things can break in favor of our mid-round targets. And the plot lines extend into the double-digit portion of the draft. However, regardless of what pick slot you get, there'll be options available to you.

The study on RB archetypes narrowed my focus down to a shorter list of candidates. Reviewing the latest ADP did the rest. And no matter where your draft slot, the blueprint doesn't really change: load up on receivers while the bell-cow well is still full, then start dipping into RBs once the position dwindles.

Sitting in an early slot? Lock in the WR tier through the first four rounds. There's more of it left at pick 4 than you'd think. Your first running back swing shouldn't come until round 5, right where a back like David Montgomery, with access to early-down and short-yardage work, is still sitting there.

Middle slots get a gift the other two don't. You can get two shots at the RB pool on the wrap in Rounds 5 and 6 while it's still worth shooting at. Or, if you'd rather, use one of those picks on a QB instead — turns out that's the best onesie value in the whole draft, RB included.

Late slot drafters get spoiled at receiver. Two full rounds pass before you pick again, so the WR run stays deep the longest. That's your strongest case for riding Zero RB the furthest — a back like Bucky Irving doesn't need to enter the conversation until Round 5, and by then your receivers have already done the heavy lifting.

Honestly, going back to the mid-round plan in the chart above, I have my concerns about the Browns' offense given their QB situation . You could persuade me to take Henderson's right-tail outcome over the median outlook for Judkins. In either case, based on the names, you can pattern-match their play styles and offenses to find similar RBs to add to your squad later.

RJ Harvey (103.5 ADP) – started in Week 2 of the preseason and capped off a drive with a 21-yard touchdown ; JK Dobbins already dealing with a minor soft-tissue injury.

Jordan Mason (116.2 ADP) – listed as co-starter alongside Aaron Jones Sr.; camp reporting indicates a bigger share of backfield touches is a possibility for '26.

MarShawn Lloyd (131.5 ADP) – taking first-team reps while Jacobs was out of training camp.

Tyjae Spears (133.3 ADP) – has matched Tony Pollard in touches and out-snapped Pollard in Week 1.

These are the type of RBs with weekly standalone value and the contingent upside should their situation change. In any other roster build, they'd be a boon for your team. But if you're already strong at WR and now you have access to an RB1 workload, that's gin.

articles.title: Micah Parsons is injured, so why did the Packers star just hit a career-high in the NFL Top 100?
articles.summary: NFL News: Micah Parsons cannot help the Green Bay Packers on the field yet. His NFL peers apparently did not need to see another snap to move him higher.Parsons.
articles.body: Micah Parsons cannot help the Green Bay Packers on the field yet. His NFL peers apparently did not need to see another snap to move him higher.Parsons landed at No. 8 in the 2026 NFL Top 100 on Wednesday, the highest placement of his five appearances on the player-voted list. The ranking comes eight months after a torn left ACL ended his first Packers season and with his 2026 return date still uncertain.Why did Micah Parsons jump to No. 8 in the NFL Top 100 after tearing his ACL?Parsons' ranking has taken a sharp turn upward.He entered the list at No. 16 in 2022, climbed to No. 9 in 2023, fell to No. 17 in 2024 and dropped to No. 36 last year. Now, after an injury-shortened season, NFL players have put him eighth.The timing might look strange. The production does not.Dallas traded Parsons to Green Bay shortly before Week 1 of the 2025 season. He responded with 12.5 sacks and 27 quarterback hits across 14 games before suffering the ACL injury against the Denver Broncos on Dec. 14.That gave Parsons at least 12 sacks in each of his first five NFL seasons. According to the Packers, he became the first player to accomplish that since sacks became an official statistic in 1982. His 65 career sacks through five seasons also rank fifth all-time over that span, one behind Hall of Famer Derrick Thomas.Parsons earned his fourth All-Pro selection and fifth consecutive Pro Bowl selection for that work.The No. 8 spot also carries some weight inside Green Bay. Parsons is the first Packers player to crack the NFL Top 100's top 10 since Aaron Rodgers ranked third in 2022. Safety Xavier McKinney, quarterback Jordan Love and running back Josh Jacobs also made this year's list at Nos. 70, 72 and 74, respectively.Seven players remain above Parsons as of Aug. 26, with the NFL revealing one name each weekday through Sept. 4.So Parsons' ranking is not a projection of what he might become after rehab. His peers voted on what he already showed before his knee gave out.Green Bay also saw what happened after losing him. The Packers finished the 2025 regular season with four consecutive losses before blowing a 21-3 halftime lead in a 31-27 NFC Wild Card loss to the Chicago Bears.That makes the next question far more important than where Parsons sits on a list.When could Micah Parsons return for the Packers, and why does Week 6 matter?Parsons has stopped short of promising a return date.Week 6, however, is sitting there for a reason.The Packers host the Dallas Cowboys at Lambeau Field on Oct. 18, giving Parsons a potential return game against the franchise that drafted him No. 12 overall in 2021 and traded him four years later.Asked earlier this month whether playing that night was realistic, Parsons told reporters:“Yeah, I think it's very realistic. We've got to do our part to make it possible. It's not off the board but we've got to put the work in.”He became more cautious about the timeline during an Aug. 10 appearance on NFL Network.“That's the most optimistic that I could be back. I could be later, there could be setbacks. Trying to integrate back into football is completely different than running on cones and ladders.”That distinction matters.Parsons underwent surgery in late December and has said his recovery comes with a firm timeline because his knee also required meniscus work. He told reporters in June that Green Bay follows a nine-month rule for his situation. The goal is to return able to finish the season, rather than simply reach the earliest available game.The Packers therefore enter 2026 knowing their highest-ranked player will not be available immediately.The NFL Top 100 vote delivered the other part of that equation Wednesday: when Parsons does return, the players who have to block him still view him as one of the eight best players in football.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Fantasy Football 2026 Consensus Mock Draft and Undervalued Sleepers to Target
articles.summary: Groupthink isn't always the most reliable voice in the fantasy football world.
articles.body:
Groupthink isn't always the most reliable voice in the fantasy football world.

That's why things like consensus rankings and average draft position data carry so much weight. They may not guarantee where players will go in a specific draft, but they do paint a pretty clear picture of a player's draft range.

To help fill in that picture, we'll lay out a three-round, 12-team PPR mock draft with each selection made by the strict guidance of consensus expert rankings featured on FantasyPros . Then, we'll close by spotlighting a couple of our favorite sleeper values for the 2026 NFL season.

3-Round, 12-Team PPR Mock Draft Using Consensus Rankings

Sleeper: Brock Purdy, QB, San Francisco 49ers

Purdy has consistently produced some of the highest fantasy points per game averages. For reasons known only to them, fantasy managers still seem skeptical of his overall profile.

On the heels of three consecutive top-10 finishes at the position, Purdy is somehow only QB13 in average draft position, per FantasyPros. There's already a bargain baked into that cost, but it might just be a ridiculous one, considering he finished the 2025 campaign as QB6 in points per game.

Is availability the worry after Purdy played only nine games last season? Maybe, but he also made 31 appearances over the previous two campaigns combined, so if that is the concern, then it's overblown.

Maybe folks don't love the age and injury risks of some of his top playmakers, but if enough of those players stay upright, Purdy will have a special collection of talent around him. Whatever the holdup, the good news is you don't have to entertain it and can just pounce on the obvious value Purdy provides.

Sleeper: Kenny Gainwell, RB, Tampa Bay Buccaneers

Gainwell was a machine down the stretch for the Pittsburgh Steelers last season. Between Weeks 11 and 18, he tallied the sixth-most PPR fantasy points at the position.

The Buccaneers clearly took notice of that. Not long after that surge, they got Gainwell's signature on a two-year, $14 million deal.

That's enough money to imagine the Buccaneers have a significant role set aside for Gainwell. Maybe the early downs still predominantly go to starter Bucky Irving, but Gainwell could handle the bulk (if not all) of the passing-down duties.

Gainwell, by the way, is good enough to challenge Irving for some of those early down snaps as well. And if Irving misses any time (he played just 10 games last season), Gainwell might have RB1 upside during any spot starts.

articles.title: NFL Free Agents 2026 Predictions for Biggest Names Left on Market
articles.summary: The preseason is coming to an end, and the NFL regular season will begin in just two weeks. While many teams are now focused on trimming rosters ahead of the August 30 cutdown day, some are still looking for fresh talent.
articles.body:
The preseason is coming to an end, and the NFL regular season will begin in just two weeks. While many teams are now focused on trimming rosters ahead of the August 30 cutdown day, some are still looking for fresh talent.

The scramble to plug roster holes has led to a late surge of free-agent activity. The list of players signed over the last month includes Jadevon Clowney, Von Miller, Stefon Diggs, Za'Darius Smith, Keenan Allen, and Derek Barnett.

While most of the top free agents are now off the market, a few notable names still linger in the available player pool. Let's take a look at some of the biggest, examine the latest buzz, and make a few predictions.

When it comes to big names left on the market, there is none bigger than Bobby Wagner. The future Hall of Famer is a six-time first-team All-Pro who has racked up 2,000 tackles over 14 seasons. He also remains a starting-caliber off-ball linebacker.

Wagner, who is the reigning Walter Payton Man of the Year, started all 17 games for the Washington Commanders last season and finished with 162 tackles, 4.5 sacks, eight tackles for loss, and two interceptions.

There is no shortage of teams that could use a defensive leader of Wagner's caliber, but the Dallas Cowboys might make the most sense. Dallas has taken an aggressive approach to rebuilding its defense this offseason—one that has included adding Miller—and head coach Brian Schottenheimer spent time with Wagner with the Seattle Seahawks.

"You're looking at one of the biggest Bobby Wagner fans in the world," Schottenheimer told Kay Adams of Up & Adams in March. "...I love that guy."

Wagner may want to skip the rigors of training camp and land with a team after roster cuts, but the 36-year-old is likely to play again in 2026. The prediction here is that he jumps from one NFC East team to another.

Offensive tackle Taylor Decker decided he'd rather walk away from the Detroit Lions than take a pay cut this offseason, and he was granted his release . He remains available and is the clear-cut top option for teams that need a starting-caliber left tackle.

While Decker has made just one Pro Bowl, he has started all 140 regular-season games in which he has appeared.

The Commanders seemed a logical landing spot for Decker, as they lost Laremy Tunsil to a torn triceps. However, Washington is hoping to replace Tunsil with an in-house option, according to ESPN's Jeremy Fowler . The Commanders have also agreed to sign D.J. Humphries, according to John Keim .

The Chicago Bears remain a sensible destination for a couple of reasons. For one, Decker played under Bears head coach Ben Johnson when Johnson was Detroit's offensive coordinator. Secondly, Chicago is still searching for a viable left tackle as Ozzy Trapilo continues to recover from a torn patellar tendon.

According to Brad Biggs of the Chicago Tribune , Braxton Jones is looking like the "clear leader" in the Bears' tackle competition, though that doesn't necessarily mean he's a quality option. Jones has not looked particularly good in limited preseason action.

Johnson is looking to craft the "highest-scoring offense ever," according to The Athletic's Dan Pompei . Don't be surprised if he turns to a familiar face to help anchor it.

Though not as much of a lock for the Hall of Fame as Wagner, wide receiver Tyreek Hill could also be Canton-bound. A four-time first-team All-Pro at wide receiver, the 32-year-old also has one Super Bowl ring and one league receiving-yardage crown.

Hill is undoubtedly a big name, but he's also coming off of a very significant knee injury that he suffered last September. The injury involved multiple torn ligaments, and Hill is still in the recovery process.

While Wagner and Decker may both be looking to sign with teams somewhere between now and Week 1, Hill may wait. According to his agent, Drew Rosenhaus, Hill is making progress but isn't in playing shape yet.

"I don't expect Tyreek to sign before the season," Rosenhaus told The Pat McAfee Show (h/t ProFootballTalk's Charean Williams ). "...He said to me, 'I still have some work to do. I'm not ready yet.'"

Hill had 21 catches for 265 yards and a touchdown in four games before the injury last season. While he may lack some of his trademark speed upon his return, he could help a contender as a complementary receiver.

Just don't expect Hill to sign until he's healthier and has a good idea of which teams are legitimate contenders.

Prediction: Hill remains unsigned through the early regular season.
